solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Explorer heads across the Atlantic heading for China: boat lost!

indicators.note: flags an American word: over there a toilet is a john
a lost boat is adrift and out of place, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: heads = toilets (naval slang); in America a toilet is a john

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A news flash about an explorer whose boat went missing on its way to China across the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: John Cabot really did sail west across the Atlantic hoping to reach Asia, so the surface is half history. A ship's toilets are its heads.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: the Venetian navigator sailed for England and reached Newfoundland in 1497.

clue.text: Card in card game, jack for opener in pontoon

indicators.note: 'X for Y' means X stands in place of Y, so the jack replaces the opener

parts.note: POKER with its opening P swapped out
the P that goes, the first letter of pontoon

explanation.surface: A card-table rule: in pontoon, a jack can stand in for the opening card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opener in pontoon' names the letter P to be replaced, not a card; pontoon is the British name for the game blackjack.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the wild extra in a pack, usually printed with a jester, is one of the cards.

clue.text: I'm hurling insults at one looking in good health!

parts.note: reads as abuse flung at someone; literally, throwing dirt in their face
reads as someone looking well; really the words of a toast, with 'looking' hinting at the eye

explanation.surface: Someone shouting abuse at a person who looks the picture of health.
explanation.walkthrough: The toast means 'good health!', but taken word for word it is someone flinging mud, which is what slinging insults is.
explanation.definitionFit: An old drinking toast, said as glasses are raised, with the same meaning as wishing someone well.

clue.text: Study standard cost for light

parts.note: to con is to study or pore over

explanation.surface: Someone researching the usual price of lighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' reads as a noun, but it is the verb: to set on fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to conflagrate is to set burning, as you ignite a fire.

clue.text: British venture I set up for powerful contractor?

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something up turns its letters to read bottom to top

parts.note: a spec is a speculative venture; set up, it becomes CEPS

explanation.surface: A British business start-up looking for a strong building contractor.
explanation.walkthrough: The contractor is not a builder but a muscle that contracts; the question mark admits the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun: muscles work by shortening, and the big upper-arm muscle is the one flexed to show strength.

clue.text: Island where three houses sound upside down

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something over makes its letters read bottom to top
the verb: a triad houses the din as a building houses people, holding it inside

parts.note: a triad is a group of three
din = a sound, turned over to NID and placed inside TRI…AD

explanation.surface: A riddle about an island where three houses make a noise upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Houses' looks like a noun counted by 'three', but it is a verb: the triad houses the reversed din.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the larger of the two Caribbean islands that form a nation with Tobago.

clue.text: Storage space costing this oddly: a hundred

indicators.note: read as 'in odd positions': keep the 1st and 3rd letters of 'this'

parts.note: T and I, the odd letters of THIS

explanation.surface: A strange price quoted for some storage space: a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' reads as 'strangely' in the surface, but it picks the odd letters of 'this'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by function: the room under a roof is where old boxes and junk get put away.

clue.text: God knows namesake Thor is furious!

indicators.note: something furious is wild and out of control, so its letters won't keep their order

explanation.surface: A god learns someone shares his name and Thor is enraged.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all Norse gods, yet 'God knows' is the everyday shrug meaning 'no idea'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two idioms with one meaning: both are shrugging replies admitting you have no idea.

clue.text: No good supporting old king, everyone together expressing disapproval

indicators.note: in a down clue, whatever supports something holds it up from underneath

parts.note: Tutankhamun, the boy pharaoh, often King Tut
musical direction for all players at once

explanation.surface: A failing regime propping up an ancient king while everyone joins in a chorus of disapproval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No good' comes first in the clue but last in the answer: supporting means underneath in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The word imitates the tongue-click sound people make when they frown on something.

clue.text: Something painful written up in pencil, occasionally

indicators.note: in a down clue, writing a word upwards makes it read bottom to top
the answer is contained in the run of letters that follows

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words: penCIL OCcasionally

explanation.surface: Someone occasionally jotting down in pencil something that hurts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' looks like an alternate-letters signal, but it is just the word the hidden letters run into.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the name for sharp abdominal cramps, familiar from crying babies.

clue.text: Loss is assigned to the past, time and time again

parts.note: 'was' is 'is' put into the past tense
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A wistful line about loss being consigned to the past, over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time and time again' is a stock phrase for 'repeatedly', but here it gives two separate times, T and AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what is wasted, spilled or worn away through use counts as lost.

clue.text: Top insect

definitions.meaning: not 'best' but the toy you set spinning
a beetle that circles fast on the surface of ponds

explanation.surface: Praise for the best bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' reads as an adjective, the best, but it is the spinning toy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from whirling: a spinning toy, and a water beetle that gyrates on ponds.

clue.text: Green cat set out to get mole

indicators.note: letters that are out are loose, set free from their order

explanation.surface: An eco-minded cat set loose in the garden to catch a mole.
explanation.walkthrough: The garden mole is a spy; 'set out' reads as one phrase but 'set' is fodder and 'out' alone the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Spy slang: a mole burrows into an organisation and works undercover from inside.

clue.text: Ladies or gents aboard raft when naked, cold

indicators.note: someone aboard a vessel is inside it
stripped of its clothes, so the outer letters R and T come off

parts.note: RAFT without its outer R and T
either is a loo; it goes aboard A…F

explanation.surface: A bare-skinned, chilly passenger on a raft looking for the toilets.
explanation.walkthrough: Ladies and gents are British names for public toilets, so a loo.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: a person who keeps apart and shows no warmth is described as chilly.

clue.text: Urge in old flame burning, lover finally bedded

parts.note: an old flame is an ex

indicators.note: put to bed inside something

parts.note: last letter of lover, bedded in HO…T

explanation.surface: A steamy scene: desire rekindled with an ex, the lover at last in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is romance throughout; 'Urge' looks like a noun (desire) but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to press someone earnestly to act.

clue.text: Stunner published, revered work

explanation.surface: A knockout book, published and venerated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stunner' suggests a beauty, but it is the punch that stuns: a KO.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the sacred scripture of Islam is a holy book held in awe.

clue.text: Game, chirpy little thing

explanation.surface: A cheerful little person ready to play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chirpy' in the surface means cheerful; here it is literal, the insect's chirp.
explanation.definitionFit: One word, two unrelated senses: the bat-and-ball sport, and the insect that rubs its wings to sing.

clue.text: Unlikely to chill, no brief garment

indicators.note: the letters as given are in an unlikely order, so find the likely one

explanation.surface: Someone wearing so little is unlikely to feel cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost fair comment: a loincloth leaves little chance to feel chilly, only overheated.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a single scanty strip wrapped round the hips covers very little.

clue.text: Value of eg real estate, real precise after negotiation

indicators.note: haggling moves the terms about, so the letters come out in a new order

explanation.surface: An estate agent's note on a property's value, precise once haggled over.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads like property jargon; 'real' appears twice, once in the definition and once as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a house sold on by its owner fetches this figure.

clue.text: Inappropriate as an idle pageboy?

definitions.meaning: out of place, not warranted, as a rude remark
read literally: a hotel page nobody has summoned

explanation.surface: A hotel bellboy lounging about, unsuitably.
explanation.walkthrough: A hotel pageboy waits to be called for; an idle one has not been, so he is literally un-called-for.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means unwarranted; the literal reading describes a page who has not been summoned.

clue.text: Music genre, grime about right

indicators.note: in the sense 'around', as in walls about a town

explanation.surface: A music-press list: the grime genre, more or less right.
explanation.walkthrough: Grime is itself a music genre, so it looks like the definition; here it only means dirt, GUNGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the 1990s Seattle rock style of Nirvana and Pearl Jam.

clue.text: Forget bottom gear trooper, you can do it!

definitions.meaning: bottom gear is underwear; slang for skipping it
read literally, a cheer urging a special-forces soldier on

explanation.surface: A driving instructor forgetting first gear, then cheering on a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom gear' reads as the lowest gear of a car; it is underwear, what covers the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang phrase means wearing no underpants; read literally, it is a shout of encouragement to a soldier.

clue.text: Drawing clear, one clarified originally after publication

indicators.note: what a word has originally is its first letter

explanation.surface: Notes on an artwork: the drawing clear, one detail clarified once it went to print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' is not a picture but the pulling a magnet does.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawing in the sense of attracting: a magnet pulls iron towards it.

clue.text: I'm into drink, time an illusion

indicators.note: something put into a drink goes inside it, so I'M sits within CH…A

parts.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone who's taken to drink finds time itself unreal.
explanation.walkthrough: Cha is British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Extended sense: the mythical fire-breathing hybrid monster became a word for any wild fancy.

clue.text: Warhol's colour frames in photos so indistinct?

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective; 'photos so indistinct' describes what it applies to

indicators.note: a frame goes round a picture

parts.note: Warhol was American, so the American spelling of grey

explanation.surface: A question about why Andy Warhol's coloured photo prints look fuzzy.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive on Warhol tells you to spell the colour his way, GRAY; 'frames' fits the art picture while meaning surround.
explanation.definitionFit: Film grain shows as visible specks in an enlarged print, making detail blurry.

clue.text: Like something off the sweet trolley — or off one's own?

definitions.text: Like something off the sweet trolley
definitions.meaning: literally: as full of nuts as a cake from the dessert trolley

explanation.surface: A restaurant dessert trolley, and someone who has left theirs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Own' takes 'trolley' from the first half: off one's trolley is British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means completely mad, and read literally describes a dessert packed with nuts.

clue.text: Antifreeze essential initially in chopper

indicators.note: what a word shows initially is its first letter

parts.note: a dicer chops food into cubes
first letter of essential, placed inside D…ICER

explanation.surface: A helicopter where antifreeze is essential.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chopper' suggests a helicopter, which really does need de-icing; it is a kitchen dicer.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonym: a spray or fluid that melts frost from windscreens and wings.

clue.text: Take a hike, as might granny?

definitions.meaning: a rude brush-off meaning go away
a granny is a kind of knot, so it is tied

explanation.surface: An elderly relative told to go away.
explanation.walkthrough: Granny is a knot, not a grandmother; 'get knotted' is British slang for 'go away'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rude dismissals telling someone to go away; a granny knot is literally tied.

clue.text: Punch consumed, a drink

parts.note: to chin someone is to punch them on the chin

explanation.surface: Someone downing a bowl of punch and a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch reads as a party drink right beside 'drink'; it is a blow, CHIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: a brew made from leaves grown in the East, often served without milk.

clue.text: Plant can drink gallon that's drained into land

indicators.note: a drained gallon has its contents poured out, leaving only its outer letters G and N
the can, drink and gallon go into the land word, sitting inside S…ETTLE

parts.note: GALLON emptied to G…N; TIN+GIN+GN goes into S…ETTLE

explanation.surface: A gardener tipping a canful of water onto soil for a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The watering picture makes 'drink' and 'drained' look like one idea; 'drained' only empties the gallon.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: a common weed whose leaves carry tiny hairs that sting.

clue.text: Pretty tree ahead

parts.note: a team two up is two ahead

explanation.surface: A lovely tree in the distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty' reads as an adjective but is the verb, as in 'pretty up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to tidy and smarten something so it looks nicer.

clue.text: Nectar collector briefly on blossom, perhaps

indicators.note: something said briefly is cut short, so BEE loses its last letter
in an across clue, a piece on another is placed after it

explanation.surface: A bee landing on a flower, possibly.
explanation.walkthrough: May is the British name for hawthorn blossom.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both adverbs express that something is possible but not certain.

clue.text: Boy in blue and reddish-brown

definitions.meaning: the boys in blue are the police

explanation.surface: A child dressed in blue and russet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boy in blue' sounds like clothing; the boys in blue are police officers.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a police officer, and the colour of the metal used in pipes and pennies.

clue.text: Rabbit and larger animal found on small islands back-to-back, eating tons

indicators.note: the two islands meet back to back, so the first is turned round to YAC
one piece eating another takes it inside

parts.note: a cay is a small low island, turned to YAC

indicators.note: in an across clue, a piece found on another comes after it

parts.note: a key is the same, as in the Florida Keys
a yak is bigger than a rabbit

explanation.surface: A bestiary: a rabbit and a bigger beast on tiny islands, munching away.
explanation.walkthrough: Rabbit here is the British verb meaning to chatter on, not the animal; the yak joins it only in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang: to rabbit on is to chatter endlessly, and the answer names that idle talk.

clue.text: Piece to hear when nocturne played?

indicators.note: the piece is one you hear rather than see, so only its sound matters

parts.note: a nocturne is evening music, played after dark

explanation.surface: A pianist asking which piece to listen to when a nocturne is on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' suggests music beside 'nocturne'; it is a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the horse-headed chessman that moves in an L shape.

clue.text: Force not creating a measure of ability to withstand compression

definitions.text: measure of ability to withstand compression

indicators.note: letters that are forced are pushed out of shape into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An engineering note about stress testing.
explanation.walkthrough: The technical surface makes 'Force' look like physics; it is the anagram instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The number on a petrol pump says how well fuel resists knocking when squeezed in the engine.

clue.text: A grotesque slur, due to cheating

indicators.note: something grotesque is distorted out of its natural shape, so the letters are too

explanation.surface: A vile slander provoked by infidelity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Due to' looks like a link to the definition, but both words are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheating in the marital sense: being unfaithful to a husband or wife.

clue.text: Difficulty with pressure cutting narrow, thin material

indicators.note: a blade cutting something goes into it

parts.note: P = pressure; ISSUE with P cuts T…APER

explanation.surface: A workshop problem: pressure cuts a narrow strip of fine material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Narrow' reads as an adjective but it is the verb TAPER, split round the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the flimsy sheets used for wrapping gifts and packing breakables.

clue.text: Duty company recalled with dispersal of riot

indicators.note: something recalled is called back
a crowd dispersed is scattered, and so are the letters of RIOT

explanation.surface: A police unit recalled from its riot-dispersal duty.
explanation.walkthrough: Octroi was a local duty on goods entering a town, once levied in France and India.
explanation.definitionFit: Duty in the tax sense: a toll charged on goods brought into a town.

clue.text: Contraption is breaking my back

indicators.note: taken back means turned round
IS breaking into the other word splits it open and sits inside

explanation.surface: A gadget causing its owner a bad back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is the exclamation, like 'oh my God!', not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, informal: any clever gadget or device whose name escapes you.

clue.text: Go and prepare a frittata?

definitions.meaning: a command to start moving, quickly
a frittata begins with eggs broken into a bowl

explanation.surface: Instructions to go and make an omelette.
explanation.walkthrough: A frittata is an Italian open omelette, so the cook must crack eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means start work at once; literally, a cook making an omelette must break eggs.

clue.text: A tad wet swimming round river… um — just stay afloat

indicators.note: letters that are swimming move about freely, so rearrange them

explanation.surface: A hesitant swimmer, slightly damp, circling a river and just managing to keep afloat.
explanation.walkthrough: The swimming scene is the definition too: treading water is staying afloat without moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Literal sense: keeping upright in deep water by pedalling the legs, going nowhere.

clue.text: A rigged trial?

parts.note: reads as fixed or cheated; really dressed in rig, in costume
reads as a court case; really a try-out run before opening night

explanation.surface: A court case with the outcome fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rigged' suggests fixed; it means kitted out, as actors are for the final run-through in costume.
explanation.definitionFit: The last full run of a play before opening, performed in costume, is a test in outfits.

clue.text: Register cheers in delight

parts.note: to register an item is to enter it

explanation.surface: Cheering loudly with joy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word but is part of the answer; ta and cheers are both British for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to amuse and please an audience or guests.

clue.text: Big deal in scrap, a dandy cut into it

indicators.note: a word that is cut loses its tail, so TOFF drops its last F

parts.note: a whit is a tiny bit
A + TOFF (a dandy) cut short, placed into WH…IT

explanation.surface: A swell getting into a scrap and making a big deal of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' suggests a fight but means a small piece; a toff is a British upper-class dandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are sarcastic shrugs dismissing something as unimportant, said to shut down a complaint.

clue.text: Little piece has nailed simply perfect thing to say

indicators.note: something nailed is pinned in place

explanation.surface: A small item has pinned down exactly the right words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nailed' fits the surface sense of getting something just right, but here it means holding in.
explanation.definitionFit: A French loan phrase, literally 'the exact word', used in English for ideal wording.

clue.text: Score's ultimately showing it?

indicators.note: the letters are on show in the words before it, visible without any rearranging

parts.note: the letters run across the two words: scoRE’S ULTimately

explanation.surface: A sports fan pointing at the scoreboard at the final whistle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' reads like a last-letter signal; here it just holds the tail of the hidden word. The whole clue is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the final scoreline displays how the match ended.

clue.text: Tablets not really working, boy almost entirely covered in spots

indicators.note: almost the entire word, so BOY loses its final letter

parts.note: BOY without its last letter, covered by PLACE…S

explanation.surface: A boy covered in spots whose medicine isn't working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' reads as a rash, which suits tablets; it means places.
explanation.definitionFit: Dummy pills with no active ingredient, given as controls in drug trials.

clue.text: Stadium reduced to dust?

explanation.surface: A stadium demolished to rubble.
explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings are a noun and a past participle, joined in a demolition picture.
explanation.definitionFit: British usage calls a sports venue this, and it is also the past tense of grind, as coffee beans.

clue.text: Sloppily inscribe second stroke

explanation.surface: A careless second pen stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stroke' fits handwriting; it is a swimming stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to write hastily and messily, in barely legible script.

clue.text: Fresh head on stick

indicators.note: a fresh version is a new one, so HEAD is remade in a new order

explanation.surface: A new tip fitted to a walking stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' reads as a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: glue and tape cling fast to a surface.

clue.text: Previously abuse someone applauding Conservative rule

explanation.surface: A political charge: past abuse of a Tory government's supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Previously' marks an archaic word: clapperclaw is an old term for scratch or revile.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic verb, found in Shakespeare, meaning to claw at or revile someone.

clue.text: Mature gorgonzola tempted you all right, every last bit

indicators.note: the last bit of every word in the run, taken together

parts.note: the final letters: gorgonzolA temptED yoU alL righT

explanation.surface: A mature cheese that tempted everyone to eat every last crumb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mature' fits the cheese, but it defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: fully grown, past childhood and adolescence.

clue.text: United team is a goal up, reportedly?

indicators.note: a report is heard rather than read, so only the sound counts

parts.note: a side a goal up is in front

explanation.surface: A football report: a united team one goal ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeds United is an English football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: one of several English football clubs with that suffix, from the Yorkshire city.

clue.text: Settler in Croatia upset about Jack residing in Dudley

indicators.note: in the sense 'around': the jumbled letters go round the rest
an upset country is tipped over, so its letters are jumbled
someone residing in a town lives inside it

parts.note: Dud, short for Dudley (as in Dudley Moore of Pete and Dud)

explanation.surface: A Croatian settler irritated over someone called Jack who lives in Dudley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settler' suggests a colonist, but it means someone who settles disputes. Dudley is also an English town, a false lead.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who settles an argument or contest: a judge, referee or arbiter.

clue.text: Fibre in light illuminated

explanation.surface: A fibre that shows up under light.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads like a lab note; the pieces are plain synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: an artificial silk spun from cellulose.

clue.text: Skim over a strategy in a crusade that saint's forsaken

indicators.note: the saint has been abandoned, so ST drops out of QUEST
the strategy goes in the crusade, sitting inside A QU…E

parts.note: A QUEST with ST (saint) left out

explanation.surface: A crusade abandoned by its saint, with a plan to glide over the problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skim over' reads as 'gloss over'; it means a car sliding over water.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyres ride up on a film of water and slide without grip, as a car does in heavy rain.

clue.text: European port tastes terrible, no stomach for it…

indicators.note: the stomach is the middle of the body, so TERRIBLE loses its middle

explanation.surface: A food critic finds a port's cuisine awful and has no appetite for it.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into 54 across, whose 'it' points back to this port.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the Adriatic harbour city in north-east Italy, near Slovenia.

clue.text: it's here, it has a lady discontented

indicators.note: read as dis-contented: LADY has its contents taken out, leaving L and Y

explanation.surface: Continuing from 53 across: the port is here, and a lady is unhappy about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' in the definition is the port from 53 across, so the answer is the country that port lies in.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross-reference: the Adriatic port in the previous clue lies within this country's borders.

clue.text: Zero transported by flier from Los Angeles further down the line

indicators.note: a passenger transported by a bird rides inside it

explanation.surface: Nothing flown in by a plane from LA, arriving later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests an aircraft beside Los Angeles; it is a bird, the tern.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for the future: at some subsequent time, eventually.

clue.text: Small show, little one

explanation.surface: A minor production starring a child.
explanation.walkthrough: A sprog is British slang for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a child, a playful term parents use for their kids.

clue.text: Tree, even hedges run through border

indicators.note: the verb: to hedge is to fence round, so E'EN encloses the border

parts.note: e'en, the poetic contraction of even
a verge is a grass border, inside E…EN
R = run in cricket, going through VERG…E

explanation.surface: A tree, with hedges running along the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hedges' is the verb, surrounding, though the garden picture makes it a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: pines, holly and yew keep their leaves all winter.
